{{Short description|Theorem in topology}}
In mathematics, '''Michael's theorem''' gives sufficient conditions for a [[regular space|regular]] [[topological space]] (in fact, for a [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub>-space]]) to be [[paracompact space|paracompact]].

== Statement ==
A family <math>E_i</math> of subsets of a topological space is said to be '''closure-preserving''' if for every subfamily <math>E_{i_j}</math>,
:<math>\overline{\bigcup E_{i_j}} = \bigcup \overline{E_{i_j}}</math>.
For example, a locally finite family of subsets has this property. With this terminology, the theorem states:<ref>{{harvnb|Michael|1957|loc=Theorem 1 and Theorem 2.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Engelking|1989|loc=Exercise 5.1.G.}}</ref> 

{{math_theorem|math_statement=Let <math>X</math> be a regular-Hausdorff topological space. Then the following are equivalent.
# <math>X</math> is paracompact.
# Each open cover has a closure-preserving refinement, not necessarily open.
# Each open cover has a closure-preserving closed refinement.
# Each open cover has a refinement that is a countable union of closure-preserving families of open sets.
}}

Frequently, the theorem is stated in the following form:

{{math_theorem|name=Corollary<ref>{{harvnb| Willard|2012|loc=Theorem 20.7.}}</ref>|math_statement= A regular-Hausdorff topological space is paracompact if and only if each open cover has a refinement that is a countable union of locally finite families of open sets.}}

In particular, a regular-Hausdorff [[Lindelöf space]] is paracompact. The proof of the theorem uses the following result which does not need regularity:

{{math_theorem|name=Proposition<ref>{{harvnb|Michael|1957|loc=§ 2.}}</ref>|math_statement=Let ''X'' be a [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub>-space]]. If ''X'' satisfies property 3 in the theorem, then ''X'' is paracompact.}}

=== Proof of Theorem from Proposition ===
Here is a proof sketch of the theorem from the proposition.

(1) <math>\Rightarrow </math> (2) trivial. (2) <math>\Rightarrow </math> (3) Since <math>X</math> is regular, we can find an open cover <math>\mathcal{V} = \{ V_x \mid x \in X \}</math> such that <math>\{ \overline{V_x} \mid x \in X \}</math> is a refinement of a given open cover <math>\mathcal U</math>. By (2), <math>\mathcal{V}</math> has a closure-preserving refinement <math>\mathcal{C}</math>. Then <math>\{ \overline{C} \mid C \in \mathcal{C} \}</math> is a refinement of <math>\mathcal{U}</math> and is clearly closure-preserving.

(3) <math>\Rightarrow </math> (4) by Proposition, and (4) <math>\Rightarrow </math> (1) again by Proposition with the aid of Lemma 2 below. <math>\square</math>

== Examples ==
Here are some examples of refinements satisfying the condition of the corollary.
*A countable open refinement trivially satisfies the condition of the corollary. Thus, a [[regular space|regular]] (Hausdorff) [[Lindelöf space]] is paracompact.
*Let <math>X</math> be a metric space and <math>U_a, a \in A</math> an open cover indexed by a well-ordered set <math>A</math>. Then let
*:<math>U_{a, n} = \{ x \mid d(x, X - U_a) > 2^{-n} \},</math>
*:<math>T_{a, n} = U_{a, n} \cap (\cap_{b < a}(X - U_b)).</math>
:Then <math>d(T_{a, n}, T_{b, n}) \ge 2^{-n}</math> for <math>b \ne a</math> and, from that, for each <math>n</math>, one can choose neighborhoods <math>V_{a, n} \supset T_{a, n}</math> inside <math>U_{a, n}</math> such that <math>\{ V_{a, n} \mid a \}</math> is locally finite.<ref>{{harvnb|Schubert|1968|loc=Ch I., § 8.7., Theorem 4.}}</ref> Then <math>\{ V_{a, n} \mid a, n \}</math> is a refinement satisfying the condition of the corollary, and we conclude <math>X</math> is paracompact.

== Proof ==

=== Lemmas ===
The proof of the proposition uses the following general lemmas:

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma 1<ref>{{harvnb|Engelking|1989|loc=Lemma 4.4.12.}}</ref> |math_statement=Let ''X'' be a topological space. If each open cover of it admits a locally finite closed refinement, then each open cover admits a locally finite open refinement (thus paracompact when ''X'' is Hausdorff).}}

''Proof'': Given an open cover <math>\mathcal{U}</math>, let <math>\mathcal{A}</math> be a locally finite closed refinement of it. By "locally finite", we can find an open cover <math>\{ V_x \mid x \in X \}</math> of <math>X</math> such that each <math>V_x</math> intersects only finitely many sets in <math>\mathcal A</math>. Then let <math>\mathcal F</math> be a locally finite closed refinement of <math>\{ V_x \mid x \}</math>. Then, for each <math>A \in \mathcal A</math>,
:<math>W(A) := \cap \{ X - F \mid F \in \mathcal{F}, \, F \cap A = \emptyset \}</math>
is an open set since <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is locally finite; thus, closure-preserving. Let <math>U : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{U}</math> be a function such that <math>A \subset U(A)</math> and then let
:<math>A' = U(A) \cap W(A),</math>
which is open. Then <math>\{ A' \mid A \in \mathcal{A} \}</math> is a locally finite open refinement of <math>\mathcal U</math> (use <math>\mathcal F</math> is a locally finite cover). <math>\square</math>

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma 2|math_statement= Let ''X'' be a topological space. Each open cover of <math>X</math> that is a countable union of locally finite collections has a locally finite refinement consisting of [[locally closed set|locally-closed set]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Engelking|1989|loc=Lemma 5.1.10.}}</ref>

Also, if <math>\mathcal{V}</math> is a countable union of closure-preserving collections of open sets, then <math>\{ \overline{V} \mid V \in \mathcal V \}</math> has a closure-preserving closed refinement.<ref>{{harvnb|Michael|1957|loc=§ 5., Proof of Theorem 2.}}</ref>}}

''Proof'': Let <math>\mathcal{U} = \cup_1^{\infty} \mathcal{U}_n</math> be an open cover that is a countable union of locally finite collections <math>\mathcal{U}_n</math>.<!-- we don’t need this, do we: Without loss of generality (i.e., not losing "locally finite"), assume <math>\mathcal{U}_n \cap \mathcal{U}_k = \emptyset, \, n \ne k.</math>--> Then let <math>U_n = \cup \mathcal{U}_n</math>, and then, for each <math>n</math> and <math>U \in \mathcal{U}_n</math>, let 
:<math>C(n, U) = U - \cup_{k < n} U_k.</math>
Then <math>\mathcal{C} := \{ C(n, U) \mid n, U \}</math> is a locally-closed cover; indeed, if <math>n</math> is the least integer such <math>x \in U_n</math>, then <math>x</math> is in some <math>U \in \mathcal{U}_n</math> and <math>x \not\in U_k, k < n</math>. For "locally finite", let <math>x</math> be in <math>X</math>; say, <math>x \in C(n, U)</math> for some <math>n, U</math>. Since each <math>\mathcal{U}_k</math> is locally finite, there is a neighborhood <math>V</math> of <math>x</math> such that <math>V</math> intersects only finitely many sets in <math>\cup_{k \le n} \mathcal{U}_k</math>. Then <math>U \cap V</math> intersects only finitely many sets in <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, since <math>U</math> is disjoint from the sets <math>C(k, W), k > n</math>. The "also" part is proved in essentially the same way; namely, given <math>\mathcal V = \cup_0^{\infty} \mathcal{V}_n</math> and <math>V_n = \cup \mathcal{V}_n</math>, let
:<math>D(n, V) = \overline{V} - \cup_{k < n} V_k.</math>
Then <math>\{ D(n, V) \mid n, V \}</math> is a required refinement. <math>\square</math>

=== Proof of Proposition ===
Let ''X'' be a T<sub>1</sub>-space in which each open cover admits a closure-preserving closed refinement.

We first note that the assumption on open covers can be strengthen to the following<ref>{{harvnb|Michael|1957|loc=Lemma 1.}}</ref>
:(*) For each open cover <math>U_i, i \in I</math>, there exists a closure-preserving closed cover <math>F_i, i \in I</math> indexed by the same <math>I</math> such that <math>F_i \subset U_i.</math>
Indeed, given such an open cover <math>U_i</math>, by assumption, we have a closure-preserving closed refinement <math>\mathcal{F}</math> of it. For each <math>i \in I</math>, let
:<math>G_i = \bigcup \{ F \in \mathcal{F} \mid F \subset U_i \}.</math>
Then this cover <math>G_i</math> has required properties.

Second, we shall note that <math>X</math> is normal.<ref>{{harvnb|Michael|1957|loc=Lemma 2.}}</ref> Indeed, given disjoint closed subsets <math>F, G</math>, the open cover <math>\{ X - F, X - G \}</math> has a closed refinement <math>\{ X - U, X - V \}</math>; say, <math>X - U \subset X - F</math> and then <math>U, V</math> are disjoint neighborhoods of <math>F, G</math>. In particular, <math>X</math> is Hausdorff since <math>X</math> is T<sub>1</sub>.

We shall now verify the hypothesis of Lemma 1. Let <math>U_a, a \in A</math> be an open cover indexed by a well-ordered set <math>A</math>. First, we shall recurviely construct a closure-preserving closed cover <math>F_{a, n}</math> as follows. For <math>n = 1</math>, let <math>F_{a, 1} \subset U_a</math> be a closed cover given by (*). Assuming we have constructed <math>F_{a, n - 1}</math>, let
:<math>U_{a, n} = U_a - \cup_{b < a} F_{b, n - 1}.</math>
It is an open cover: if <math>a</math> is the least element with the property <math>x \in F_{a, {n-1}} \subset U_a</math>, then <math>x \not\in F_{b, n - 1}, b < a</math> and so <math>x \in U_{a, n}</math>. By (*), let <math>F_{a, n} \subset U_{a, n}</math> be a closure-preserving closed cover.

Now, since <math>X = F_{a, n} \cup (\cup_{b \ne a} F_{b. n})</math>, we have:
:<math>V_{a, n} := X - (\cup_{b \ne a} F_{b, n}) \subset F_{a, n},</math>
which is open since <math>\{ F_{a, n} \mid a, n \}</math> is closure-preserving. We claim <math>\{ V_{a, n} \mid a, n \}</math> is an open ''cover''. Let <math>x \in X</math> and for each <math>n</math>, let <math>a_n</math> be the least element such that <math>x \in F_{a_n, n}</math>. We have <math>a_1 \ge a_2 \ge \cdots</math> since <math>F_{a, n} \cap F_{b, n - 1} = \emptyset, b < a</math>. Since <math>A</math> is well-ordered, the sequence <math>a_n</math> cannot be strictly decreasing all the way; i.e., <math>a_{n - 1} = a_n</math> for some <math>n</math> and then similarly we see <math>x \not\in F_{b, n}, b \ne a_n.</math> That is, <math>x</math> is in <math>V_{a_n, n}</math>. Note also <math>V_{a, n} \cap V_{b, n} = \emptyset, b \ne a.</math>

Finally, by (*), we can find a closure-preserving closed refinement <math>D_{a, n} \subset V_{a, n}</math>. By normality, we then find open sets <math>W_{a, n}</math> such that
:<math>D_{a, n} \subset W_{a, n} \subset \overline{W_{a, n}} \subset V_{a, n}.</math>
For each <math>n</math>, let <math>U_n</math> be the union of all open sets, each of which intersects only finitely many sets in <math>\{ W_{a, n} \mid a \}</math>. It is a neighborhood of <math>D_n := \cup_a D_{a, n}</math> since <math>\{ W_{a, n} \mid a \}</math> is a disjoint collection. By normality, we have neighborhoods <math>U'_n</math> of <math>D_n</math> with closures lying in <math>U_n</math>.
Then let
:<math>W_{a, n}' = W_{a, n} \cap U_n'.</math>
Then <math>\{ W_{a, n}' \mid a \}</math> is locally finite. Thus, by Lemma 2, we find a locally finite locally-closed refinement <math>\mathcal{C}</math> of <math>\{ W_{a, n}' \mid a, n \}.</math> Then, since passing to closure doesn’t spoil “locally finite", <math>\{ \overline{C} \mid C \in \mathcal{C}  \}</math> is a refinement satisfying the hypothesis of Lemma 1. (The argument after "finally" except Lemma 2 is essentially due to Dowkey.<ref>p. 308 in Dowker, C.H., 1952. On a theorem of Hanner. Arkiv för Matematik, 2(4), pp.307-313.</ref>) <math>\square</math>

== Similar result ==
There is a similar result due to A. H. Stone (which was actually used to prove a metric space is paracompact).

{{math_theorem|name=Proposition<ref>{{harvnb|Willard|2012|loc=Theorem 20.14.}}</ref>|math_statement=Let ''X'' be a [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub>-space]]. Then each open cover admits a barycentric open refinement (defined below) if and only if ''X'' is paracompact.}}

Given a set <math>X</math> and a cover <math>\mathcal{C}</math> of it, for each element <math>x \in X</math>, we write
:<math>\operatorname{St}(x, \mathcal{C}) = \bigcup \{ C \in \mathcal{C} \mid x \in C \},</math>
and call it the [[star (topology)|star]] over <math>x</math> with respect to <math>\mathcal C</math>. A collection <math>\mathcal D</math> of subsets of <math>X</math> is then called a '''barycentric refinement''' of <math>\mathcal C</math> if <math>\{ \operatorname{St}(x, \mathcal{D}) \mid x \in X \}</math> is a refinement of <math>\mathcal C</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Engelking|1989|loc=Just before Theorem 5.1.12.}}</ref> A barycentric refinement is in particular a refinement.

Lemma 1 is then strengthened to<ref>{{harvnb|Engelking|1989|loc=Remark 5.1.14.}}</ref> 
*If each open cover has a locally finite closed refinement, then each open cover has a locally finite barycentric open refinement.

The proof of the other direction of the theorem uses the following idea: construct a sequence of successive barycentric refinements
:<math>\mathcal{U}_0 \succ \mathcal{U}_1 \succ \mathcal{U}_2 \succ \cdots</math>
where <math>\mathcal{U}_0 := \mathcal{U}</math> is the given open cover <math>\mathcal{U}</math> and we wrote <math>\prec</math> for a barycentric refinement. Very roughly, this puts us in a setup similar to the metric-space one discussed at {{section link||Examples}} and we finish the proof similarly (the actual details are more involved).
